title: Arbitrage: Hard to Find in Finance, and Easy to Find in Healthcare?
subtitle: The Most Premium Content
body_html:
Arbitrage is a popular term in finance circles. It means you can buy one thing and then immediately sell it to somebody else for more than you bought it. It's the perfect product because it is essentially a glitch in the matrix. The literal dictionary definition is as follows:

“the simultaneous buying and selling of securities, currency, or commodities in different markets or in derivative forms to take advantage of differing prices for the same asset.”

Finding these opportunities in markets is relatively rare because everyone is looking.

For reasons that escaped me, very similar opportunities exist in healthcare. Most are instant like you can get out of a literal arbitrage opportunity in a capital market. So there's some us to find and execute on these healthcare discrepancies.

Essentially, they're all over the place.

There is a company called Neuronetics. It makes transcranial magnetic stimulation devices.

I won't talk in detail about their technology or lack thereof.

I will point out that the core technology, the figure of 8 coils, is not protected by patent.

Neuronetics sells transcranial magnetic stimulation devices for X dollars and then attaches a paper-use charge to every treatment delivered.

It used to be $70 a treatment. I honestly don't know what it is now. But it is something.

There are a gazillion manufacturers that make close to the identical device. MagStim, MagVenture, cloud TMS, I can go on and on. Brainsway way also makes TMS devices, but for reasons I won't bother to get into, they have patented technology that is somewhat different.

The critical thing to understand is that the market leader in the space is a publicly traded company. And it's getting paid $70, or something, every time someone gets treated with one of their devices.

One course of treatment for depression is 36 treatments. At Medicare rates, providers are getting something like 200 bucks per treatment.

There is no benefit to continuing to treat patients with a neuronetics branded coil vs. any other coil. Now, that's an opinion when it comes to science, and I can defend it all day long. But I'm not making that argument in this article. Instead, the argument I'm making is a financial one.

For a treatment that, per patient, reimburses something like 7,200 per 36 treatments, and we're talking about something as common as depression, getting paid (net) less than $2,520 per patient is dumb.

Now there are plenty of reasons individual practitioners might choose to stay in that arrangement. However, that is different from what I'm writing about.

They're going to help with marketing. I like the sales rep. They threw the best parties at the conference. Their advertising is slick. Whatever. You can tell yourself any story you want as an individual provider.

Here's the thing I fundamentally don’t understand: Neuronetics is a public company. It is essentially a brand name kleenex in a world full of facial tissue.

Its devices cost something like $150,000. Sometimes more, sometimes a lot less. It doesn't matter.

Let's imagine you wanted to buy some stock options…but at least right now, it's worth noting the company has a market cap of 149m.

Now, follow me for the magic trick that is an arbitrage opportunity in healthcare.

For my readers who are not hustlers in capital markets, I will find something that will make the whole thing and make a lot more. Just like you can buy and sell shares of a stock, you can buy and sell contracts to buy and sell shares of a stock in the future. So you can place bets on a stock's share price going up or down.

Now, usually, you can't know in advance what will happen to the share price of a stock because that would be insider knowledge! But there are such things as short sellers, who will place very extensive bets on a share price going up or down, and then, like the Hindenburg report, publicize their research, just like I'm doing right now, in the hopes that the market will follow their advice, and thus make a lot of money.

But here's what I don't get, in an arbitrage opportunity, if you can see it, you can take it. So there is nearly nothing preventing you from capitalizing on an arbitrage opportunity because you can buy and sell the thing simultaneously—and since people are looking for these things constantly if they exist, they don't last very long. Because why would that be a thing?

Neuronetics presents such an opportunity.

The first thing you could do is buy Puts (these are contracts to sell shares). There are more Sophisticated ways to do this, but I’m illustrating a point.

So you can see that what happens is that if the share price falls, you can then make money because you are buying a contract to sell that stock at a price that would be higher than its actual price to purchase it. So you can see that happens if the share price falls; you can make money because you are buying a contract to sell that stock at a price that would be higher than its actual price to purchase it. So you're generating an arbitrage opportunity in the future for yourself!

But there's no free lunch; how can you ensure that that's the direction the share price will go?

Magic!

What would happen if you took every clinic using one of these machines and swapped out their current device with a device that didn't cost them any money? Don’t charge them; give it to them!

With the above bet, if the share price went to zero, you could make 117.5m.

For 100,000,000 million, you could buy 1000 TMS machines at 100k each. And give them to clinics using neuronetics machines. This would tank their revenue source. No more paper fees, every clinic is making 2500+ more dollars every time they do a treatment for somebody with depression, and you have cut the spigot of revenue into a publicly traded company, which on the next earnings call would have to report that they lost a bunch of money. Overnight. Assuming it craters the company entirely, you'd walk away with $17 million.

There are ways to do that with zero upfront capital, by the way. But I'm not going to go into the details.

It is free money. For the life of me, I can't understand why this hasn’t happened.

This is just one example not investment advice, and this is just one example, it's not investment advice, and I don't have the money to do it, so I'm just telling you you could.

There are a bazillion opportunities like this in healthcare where things are just so bizarrely mispriced this could be your whole job. People spend an entire career trying to find tiny fractions of percent differences in markets. In healthcare, there's 4.6 trillion of spending, much of which is so poorly allocated…it could be dealt with overnight.

So please, financiers, join me in driving the cost of healthcare down; the water is warm.

—Owen Scott Muir, M.D.
